Four drum machines shaped most of the beats of the last forty-five years. The **Roland TR-808** (1980) and **TR-909** (1983)
built their drums from circuits; the **LinnDrum** (1982) played recordings of real drums; the **Akai MPC60** (1988) played any
sound you sampled into it, with timing you could leave exactly as you played it. On this page each one is rebuilt in the
browser. Program a beat on one, turn it into another, and read what happened to every drum, knob and note:
**the same**, **close** or **impossible**, and why.

The panels are drawn after the real machines and are not copies; the names belong to their makers. Every fact about the
machines comes from their manuals (cited with the page) or from Wikipedia. What the manuals do not say, such as how much a
909 shuffle setting moves a note, is this page's own choice and is marked so. **The sounds are stand-ins**: the 808 and 909
drums are synthesised after the circuit descriptions; the 909's sampled hats and cymbals, and every LinnDrum and MPC sound,
are synthesised and then cut to the machine's bit depth and sample rate. Nobody has compared them with the real machines.

## The machines

<div class="dcmp"></div>

**How to use it.** Pick an **Example**, then **▶ A**, **▶ B** or **▶ A, then B**. Click a step on panel A to add a hit;
click again for an accent, a higher level, a louder velocity or (909) a flam ≀. Change machine with the menu on either
panel. **Make this the starting point** turns the translation into the new source. Point at a line of the report to light
up the rows and knobs it is about. Outlines show <span class="dcmp-key dcmp-exact">the same</span>,
<span class="dcmp-key dcmp-approx">close</span> and <span class="dcmp-key dcmp-lost">cannot be done</span>.

## Steps, accents and swing

| | TR-808 | TR-909 | LinnDrum | MPC60 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Grid | 1-32 steps a measure, 16 by default (Service Notes p. 1; owner's manual) | 16ths or triplets, last step 1-16 (manual p. 24) | error correct 1/8 to 1/32 triplet, or HI = as played (p. 7) | timing correct 1/8 to 1/32 triplet, or OFF = 96 parts per quarter note (pp. 26, 43) |
| Loudness | one accent row for the whole step, 0-10 dB (SN p. 1) | total accent, plus accents on bass drum, snare, toms and closed hat (p. 25) | 3 levels on snare, 2 on bass, hi-hat, cabasa, tambourine, ride (p. 1) | velocity; 16 Levels plays one sound at 16 velocities (pp. 21-22) |
| Swing | none described | shuffle 1-7 on 16ths (p. 26) | timing A (straight) to F (shuffle), on 8ths or 16ths; E = perfect triplet (pp. 8-9) | Swing 50-75 %, 66 % = triplet (p. 44) |
| Flam | no | 8 intervals on bass, snare, toms; first hit on the step (p. 26) | no | no (two notes) |

The **timing plot** under the panels draws where every hit of A (above) and B (below) lands; a short line from a dot to the
grid shows how far swing or hand-played timing has moved it. Try **MPC beat, swing 62 %** into the 909: all the late
snares jump back onto the steps. The MPC manual itself suggests 54 % for 16th hi-hats and 62 % for a relaxed 16th swing
(MPC60 manual p. 44). Roger Linn, who wrote the LinnDrum's timing settings, also wrote the MPC60 manual; its percentages
are the clearest statement of what "swing" means on these machines: the share of each pair of notes given to the first.

## Sounds and knobs

- **TR-808.** Every drum is a circuit. The bass drum is a "bridged T-network" that rings when struck; with an accent its
  time constant is halved for 4 ms, so it starts at twice its frequency, a "punchier crisp bass" (Service Notes p. 5). The
  cowbell is two square-wave oscillators; the cymbal and hi-hats share six; a closed hat cuts the open one off (p. 6).
  Toms and congas share circuits, chosen by a switch, so one pattern cannot use both a low tom and a low conga (p. 6).
- **TR-909.** Bass drum with tune, attack and decay, snare with tune, tone and snappy, toms with tune and decay (manual
  p. 8). Wikipedia: its crash, ride and hi-hats are 6-bit samples made by Atsushi Hoshiai; the rest are analog.
- **LinnDrum.** Recordings of drums (8-bit, 28-35 kHz, Wikipedia). Only the snare, sidestick, toms and congas tune, by
  about an octave, and the closed hi-hat has a decay knob; "all other drums are not tunable" (manual p. 1).
- **MPC60.** Any sound sampled into it, 12-bit at 40 kHz (manual p. 15), with envelope, tuning and velocity settings for
  each pad (p. 5).

Under the panels, pick a **voice** to see its waveform, its loudness envelope and its spectrum on both machines.

## TR-808: history, music, records

Roland made the TR-808 from 1980 to 1983; it cost US$1,195. A team led by Tadao Kikumoto designed it, with Makoto Muroi,
Hiro Nakamura (voice circuits) and Hisanori Matsuoka. It makes its sounds by analog synthesis, not samples. Users program
up to 32 patterns, chain up to 768 measures and place accents on beats. It was a commercial failure; about 12,000 were
made. It became a foundation of hip-hop and was used across electronic and dance music, Miami bass, Detroit techno and R&B.

Records and players: Yellow Magic Orchestra played it live on "1000 Knives" at the Budokan in 1980 and used it on *BGM*
(1981); Ryuichi Sakamoto's *B-2 Unit* and "Riot in Lagos"; Marvin Gaye's "Sexual Healing" (1982), the first US hit with
the 808; Afrika Bambaataa & the Soulsonic Force's "Planet Rock" (1982); the Beastie Boys' "Paul Revere" (1986, a reversed
808); Whitney Houston's "I Wanna Dance With Somebody" (1987); Kanye West's *808s & Heartbreak* (2008); Run-DMC, LL Cool J
and Public Enemy (all from Wikipedia, "Roland TR-808").

## TR-909: history, music, records

Made 1983-85 at US$1,195, again led by Tadao Kikumoto. Its voices are analog except the crash, ride and hi-hats, 6-bit
samples by Atsushi Hoshiai; it was Roland's first drum machine with samples and with MIDI. It chains up to 96 patterns
into songs of up to 896 measures, with shuffle, flam and accents. About 10,000 were built and it was a commercial
failure, but second-hand 909s became central to techno, house and acid house: Derrick May, Frankie Knuckles, Jeff Mills.
Records: Adamski's "Killer" (1990), Daft Punk's "Revolution 909" (*Homework*, 1997), Björk's "Hunter" (1997), Radiohead's
"Videotape" (2007) (Wikipedia, "Roland TR-909").

## LinnDrum: history, music, records

Linn Electronics made the LinnDrum from 1982 to 1985; Roger Linn designed it. It cost US$2,995 and about 5,000 were sold.
It plays 8-bit samples at 28-35 kHz from 15 pads. Wikipedia gives 56 user and 42 preset patterns; the owner's manual read
here numbers 49 patterns, those starting 1-5 preset (p. 2), so models or software versions may differ (unverified).
Users included Trevor Horn (Sound On Sound's "Classic Tracks" on "Relax"), Mark Knopfler, George Michael, Naked Eyes and
Stock Aitken Waterman (Wikipedia, "LinnDrum").

## Akai MPC: history, music, records

The MPC60 came out on 8 December 1988 at $5,000, designed by Roger Linn with David Cockerell's team at Akai, with a 4 x 4
grid of pressure-sensitive pads. DJ Shadow made *Endtroducing* (1996) on an MPC60 MkII; J Dilla turned the quantize off
for his off-kilter feel; Kanye West made *The College Dropout* (2004) and played "Runaway" live on an MPC2000XL (2010)
(Wikipedia, "Akai MPC"). The later MPC3000 is not covered here: no manual for it has been read for this page.

## Rebuild a beat from a video

Watch one of the videos below, rebuild the beat on the matching machine, then **⤓ Export JSON**: fill in the song,
artist, the video's address, channel and title and the time in the video where the beat is shown, and save the file.
**⤒ Import JSON** opens a file again (yours or a classmate's) on its own machine; then turn it into the others. The file
holds `kind: "drum-pattern"`, `version: 1`, the machine, its kit, the pattern, the song and the source. Each video was
checked to exist on 25 November 2026; what each shows is as its title says.

## What is checked and what is not

Checked against the manuals: each machine's instruments and knobs, step counts and scales, accents and levels, the 909's
shuffle settings and flams, the LinnDrum's error-correct and timing settings (only A = straight and E = triplet as amounts),
the MPC60's timing correct, swing percentages, 96 ppq and 16 Levels, and the 808's voice circuits as the service notes
describe them. Each report line names its page.

This page's own choices: every sound (synthesised stand-ins, including the 808 cymbal and cowbell frequencies); knob curves;
how far 909 shuffle 2-7 and LinnDrum timing B, C, D and F move a note; the 909's flam intervals in ms; the 85 % velocity
that becomes an accent; which 808 pre-scale gives triplets. Nobody has compared these sounds with the real machines.
